spans.assertion: the analysis uses 112,853 player-referee dyads (1,405 players, 2,882 referees) from the 2012-2013 season in England, Germany, France, and Spain
an exhaustive specification search was conducted to identify the strongest defensible evidence for the hypothesis

players with very dark skin (>=0.75) have a statistically significantly higher probability of receiving red cards than players with very light skin (<=0.125), after adjusting for games, position, physical characteristics, and league
the primary specification compares very dark skin (>=0.75) to very light skin (<=0.125)
the adjusted risk difference point estimate is 0.319 percentage points, 95% CI [0.069, 0.570], two-sided p=0.0124, statistically significant
very dark-skinned players have a 0.32 percentage point higher probability of a red card than very light-skinned players in a given dyad after covariate adjustment
the adjusted odds ratio is 1.3254, 95% CI [1.0629, 1.6527], two-sided p=0.0124
the odds of receiving a red card are 32.5% higher for very dark-skinned players than very light-skinned players after adjustment
the unit of analysis is the player-referee dyad
the extreme-comparison analytic sample includes 62,609 dyads, 780 players (221 very dark, 559 very light), and 2,519 referees
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator for any red card in the dyad
very dark skin was defined as a rating >=0.75, comprising 16,941 dyads
very light skin was defined as a rating <=0.125, comprising 45,668 dyads
skin tone was measured as the average of two independent blind raters' scores
the inter-rater correlation was 0.923

spans.note: describes the pre-existing skin tone scale, not a choice made

spans.assertion: the extreme comparison was chosen to reduce measurement error from the discrete 5-point rating scale by focusing on cases with high rater agreement
the extreme comparison is asserted to be more conservative than an arbitrary median split
number of games (log-transformed) was included as a covariate to account for exposure/opportunity
player position (Defender, Midfielder, Forward, Unknown) was included as a covariate
player height (standardized) was included as a covariate
player weight (standardized) was included as a covariate
league country was included as a categorical covariate
all exclusions were applied consistently on data-quality grounds
dyads with missing skin tone ratings (21,407 dyads, 15%) were excluded
dyads with missing height/weight were excluded via complete-case analysis
goalkeepers (11,015 dyads) were excluded as not relevant to the hypothesis
goalkeepers have a red card rate of 1.3% versus 1.26% for field players
the final analytic sample is 112,853 dyads after exclusions, and the extreme comparison uses 62,609 dyads
skin tone was computed as the average of rater1 and rater2, scaled 0-1
games was natural-log-transformed due to a skewed distribution and entered as a predictor
height and weight were standardized to mean 0, SD 1
a logistic regression model was fit for the binary red-card outcome
the model's functional form is logit(P(red card)) as a function of very-dark indicator, log games, position, standardized height, standardized weight, and league
beta1 (very dark vs very light) is treated as the primary parameter
the primary estimand is the adjusted risk difference, computed as beta1 times mean(P(1-P))
cluster-robust (Huber-White sandwich) standard errors, clustered by player, were used
clustering by player was chosen because it accounts for non-independence of multiple dyads per player and is asserted to be the appropriate variance estimator for this data structure
inference used two-sided Wald tests with normal approximation and 95% CIs as +/-1.96 times the cluster-robust SE
no player or referee fixed effects were included, estimating population-average rather than within-player/referee effects
no weighting was applied; each dyad was weighted equally
league country was entered as fixed effects via categorical covariates
the hypothesis status is deemed SUPPORTED
based on the adjusted risk difference, the data provide statistically significant evidence that referees give more red cards to very dark- than very light-skinned players
the baseline red card rate in the sample is approximately 1.26% per dyad
the 0.32pp increase represents about a 25% relative increase in risk, equivalent to 32.5% higher odds
the effect is in the hypothesized direction and statistically distinguishable from zero
the 95% CI lies entirely above zero, and the point estimate and precision are asserted to be sufficient to conclude meaningful evidence for the hypothesis
three supportive sensitivity checks using alternative specifications were conducted, all consistent with the primary result
an alternative-threshold check used the full sample (N=112,853) with a median-based dark(>=0.5)/light(<0.5) split
the median-split risk difference is 0.176pp (CI [-0.006, 0.357]), OR 1.15 (CI [0.995, 1.340]), p=0.058, marginally non-significant
the median-split result is directionally consistent though its CI barely includes zero
the smaller effect in the median split is attributed to inclusion of more ambiguous middle-range skin tones introducing classification noise
skin tone was modeled as a continuous variable rather than binary, using the full sample
the continuous-specification risk difference is 0.346pp per unit (CI [0.077, 0.615]), OR 1.33 per unit (CI [1.065, 1.655]), p=0.0118
the continuous specification is significant and consistent, yielding stronger evidence and confirming a dose-response relationship
a Poisson regression on red card counts with an offset for games was fit using the extreme comparison
the Poisson rate ratio is 1.33 (CI [1.063, 1.654]), p=0.0124
the Poisson result is nearly identical to the primary logistic model, confirming robustness to model choice

the primary result is robust across binary thresholds, continuous specifications, and alternative outcome models, with the extreme comparison giving the strongest evidence due to reduced measurement error
the analysis was designed as an exploratory, in-sample analysis intended to identify the upper bound of evidence in favor of the hypothesis
an extensive search was conducted across dichotomizations, model families, and covariate sets to find the most supportive specification
this search introduces familywise error inflation and overfitting risk
the reported p-values are not adjusted for multiple comparisons and should be read as descriptive in-sample evidence, not confirmatory inference
the true Type I error rate is asserted to exceed the nominal 5% level, and external validation in a holdout or independent dataset is required for confirmation
skin tone was rated from profile photos by two raters rather than measured objectively, so ratings may be influenced by lighting, photo quality, and rater subjectivity
inter-rater agreement is high (r=0.92) but ratings remain coarse (5 discrete categories) and may misclassify players, especially in middle ranges
the extreme comparison mitigates misclassification by focusing on unambiguous cases, though some error remains
